lessons.title: Homeostasis and the Nervous System
lessons.description: How homeostasis, receptors, neurones, synapses, and reflex arcs keep the body stable.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism. The goal is to maintain optimum conditions for function — the best possible environment for enzyme action and all cell processes — despite constant changes happening both inside and outside the body.

The human body must keep several internal conditions within narrow limits. These include blood glucose concentration, body temperature, and water levels. If any of these drift too far from the optimum, enzymes cannot work efficiently, chemical reactions slow down or stop, and cells can be damaged or destroyed.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains optimal conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions. Without it, enzymes would denature and metabolic reactions would fail.

Control Systems

All homeostatic control systems — whether nervous or chemical — share three essential components. You must know these for the exam:

1. Receptors — cells that detect stimuli (changes in the environment). For example, temperature receptors in the skin detect when you touch something hot. 2. Coordination centres — such as the brain, spinal cord, and pancreas — that receive and process information from receptors. 3. Effectors — muscles or glands that bring about responses to restore optimum levels.

The body uses two types of automatic control system. Nervous responses are fast, short-lived, and travel as electrical impulses along neurones (e.g. pulling your hand away from a flame). Chemical (hormonal) responses are slower, longer-lasting, and travel in the blood (e.g. insulin controlling blood glucose). Both work through the same receptor → coordinator → effector pathway, but the speed and duration differ.

The Nervous System

The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour. It detects changes in the environment using receptors, processes the information, and triggers appropriate responses.

Information from receptors passes along specialised cells called neurones as electrical impulses. These impulses travel to the central nervous system (CNS), which is made up of the brain and spinal cord. The CNS acts as the coordination centre — it processes the information and coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

Key Fact

The nervous pathway follows this sequence: \(stimulus \rightarrow receptor \rightarrow coordinator (CNS) \rightarrow effector \rightarrow response\). Learn this order — it appears in almost every exam question on this topic.

Types of Neurone

There are three types of neurone, each with a specific role in the nervous pathway:

Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. They have a long axon and a cell body branching off to one side. Relay neurones are found entirely within the CNS. They connect sensory neurones to motor neurones and allow the brain or spinal cord to process information. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors. They have a long axon and a cell body at one end with branching dendrites.

Synapses

Neurones do not physically touch each other. There is a tiny gap between them called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of one neurone, it triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters. These chemicals diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. This process converts an electrical signal into a chemical signal and back again.

Neurotransmitters are only released from one side of the synapse (the pre-synaptic neurone) and can only bind to receptors on the other side (the post-synaptic neurone). This means impulses can only travel in one direction, ensuring signals reach the correct destination. Some drugs and toxins work by mimicking or blocking neurotransmitters at synapses.

Reflex Actions

A reflex action is an automatic and rapid response to a stimulus. Reflex actions do not involve the conscious part of the brain — they are coordinated by the spinal cord. This makes them much faster than voluntary responses, which is essential for protecting the body from harm.

Examples include pulling your hand away from a hot plate, your pupil constricting in bright light, and blinking when an object moves towards your eye.

Key Fact

The reflex arc pathway is: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector. Reflex actions bypass the conscious brain, making them automatic and fast enough to prevent injury.

1. The stimulus is heat from the hot plate. 2. Temperature receptors in the skin detect the heat. 3. An electrical impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord. 4. The impulse passes across a synapse to a relay neurone in the spinal cord. 5. The impulse passes across another synapse to a motor neurone. 6. The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector — a muscle in the arm. 7. The muscle contracts (response), pulling the hand away before the brain has even registered the pain.

Reaction Time

Reaction time is the time it takes for a person to respond to a stimulus. In humans, typical reaction times are between 0.2 and 0.9 seconds. Reaction time can be measured using a simple ruler-drop test — this is Required Practical 7 in the AQA specification.

Factors that can affect reaction time include age, gender, caffeine, tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions. In the required practical, students investigate the effect of one factor (such as practice or distraction) on human reaction time using a ruler-drop method, then calculate the mean to improve reliability.

Method: One person holds a ruler vertically at the 0 cm mark. A second person places their thumb and finger around the ruler at the 0 mark without touching it. The ruler is released without warning, and the catcher grabs it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls (in cm) is recorded. This is repeated at least 5 times and the mean distance is calculated.

Key points: The further the ruler falls, the slower the reaction time. To make it a fair test, the same ruler and same hand position should be used each time. Anomalous results (e.g. if the person anticipates the drop) should be identified and excluded before calculating the mean.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For AQA Trilogy questions on this topic, always use the correct sequence: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response. In “explain” questions about reflex arcs, name each type of neurone and describe what happens at each synapse. For “describe” questions about reaction time practicals, remember to mention calculating the mean and identifying anomalous results — examiners expect these terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions (blood glucose, temperature, water levels) to maintain optimum conditions for enzyme action. All control systems use receptors, coordination centres, and effectors.
  • The nervous system transmits electrical impulses along sensory, relay, and motor neurones. Synapses transmit signals chemically between neurones using neurotransmitters.
  • Reflex actions are automatic, rapid responses that bypass the conscious brain (receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector), protecting the body from harm.

lessons.title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control
lessons.description: How hormones coordinate body functions, with a focus on insulin, glucagon and diabetes.
lessons.content_html:
The Human Endocrine System

The endocrine system is made up of glands that produce chemicals called hormones. Unlike electrical impulses in the nervous system, hormones are carried in the blood to their target organs, where they produce a response.

The endocrine system works more slowly than the nervous system, but its effects are longer lasting. Nervous responses happen in milliseconds and are short-lived. Hormonal responses take seconds to minutes to begin but can last for hours, days, or even longer.

Key Fact

The nervous system produces fast, short-lived responses using electrical impulses. The endocrine system produces slower, longer-lasting responses using chemical messengers (hormones) carried in the blood.

The Major Endocrine Glands

You need to know the main glands, the hormones they produce, and the role of each hormone. The pituitary gland sits at the base of the brain and is often called the “master gland” because it secretes several hormones that act on other glands, stimulating them to produce their own hormones.

Pituitary gland (brain): The master gland — produces hormones including FSH and LH that stimulate other glands. It controls growth, reproduction, and water balance.

Thyroid gland (neck): Produces thyroxine, which controls the body’s metabolic rate — how quickly cells convert food into energy.

Adrenal glands (above kidneys): Produce adrenaline, the “fight or flight” hormone, released in response to stress or danger.

Pancreas (abdomen): Produces insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose levels.

Ovaries (female): Produce oestrogen, which controls the menstrual cycle and female secondary sexual characteristics. Testes (male): Produce testosterone, which controls male secondary sexual characteristics.

Control of Blood Glucose Concentration

The blood glucose level must be kept within a narrow range. If it rises too high or drops too low, cells cannot function properly — enzymes rely on stable conditions. The pancreas is the organ that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration.

After you eat a meal, carbohydrates are digested into glucose. This glucose is absorbed into the blood, causing blood glucose levels to rise. The pancreas detects this rise and responds by releasing insulin into the blood.

Key Fact

Insulin lowers blood glucose by causing body cells to take up glucose from the blood, and by causing the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage. Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles.

What Happens When Blood Glucose Is Too Low (Higher Tier)

If blood glucose levels fall too low — for example, during exercise or between meals — the pancreas detects this drop and releases the hormone glucagon. Glucagon travels in the blood to the liver, where it causes glycogen to be converted back into glucose. This glucose is then released into the blood, raising the blood glucose level back to normal.

Insulin and glucagon work together as an antagonistic pair — they have opposite effects. This is an example of negative feedback, where a change in conditions triggers a response that reverses that change, bringing the system back to its normal level.

Blood glucose too high: Pancreas detects the rise → pancreas releases insulin → insulin causes cells to absorb glucose and liver to convert glucose to glycogen → blood glucose falls back to normal → pancreas reduces insulin secretion.

Blood glucose too low: Pancreas detects the drop → pancreas releases glucagon → glucagon causes liver to convert glycogen back to glucose → glucose released into blood → blood glucose rises back to normal → pancreas reduces glucagon secretion.

This cycle repeats continuously, keeping blood glucose levels stable. The key idea is that the response reverses the change — that is what makes it negative feedback.

Negative Feedback and Thyroxine (Higher Tier)

Negative feedback also controls thyroxine levels. When thyroxine levels in the blood are too low, the pituitary gland releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which stimulates the thyroid gland to produce more thyroxine. As thyroxine levels rise, the pituitary gland detects this and reduces TSH production, so the thyroid produces less thyroxine. This keeps thyroxine — and therefore metabolic rate — stable.

Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in response to fear, stress, or excitement. It prepares the body for “fight or flight” by increasing heart rate, diverting blood flow to the muscles, and raising blood glucose levels (by causing glycogen to be broken down). Adrenaline release is controlled by the nervous system rather than by negative feedback — it is a rapid, short-term response.

Key Fact — Negative Feedback

Negative feedback is a control mechanism where a change in conditions triggers a response that reverses that change, restoring the system to its normal level. Both blood glucose (insulin/glucagon) and thyroxine (TSH) are controlled by negative feedback.

Diabetes

Diabetes is a condition where the body cannot control blood glucose levels properly. There are two types, and the exam will expect you to compare them clearly.

Type 1 diabetes occurs when the pancreas does not produce insulin. The immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells. Without insulin, blood glucose levels can rise to dangerously high levels after eating.

Treatment: Insulin injections, usually several times a day. The person must carefully monitor their blood glucose levels and adjust their insulin dose based on what they eat and their activity levels. There is no cure — this is a lifelong condition.

Cause: It is thought to be an autoimmune condition — the body’s own immune system attacks the pancreas cells. It usually develops in childhood or young adulthood and is not linked to lifestyle.

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body’s cells no longer respond to insulin properly — this is called insulin resistance. The pancreas may still produce insulin, but it has little effect. Blood glucose levels can therefore rise dangerously.

Treatment: A carbohydrate-controlled diet and regular exercise. Some patients may also need medication. Unlike Type 1, it does not usually require insulin injections (although some severe cases may).

Risk factors: Obesity is the major risk factor. A sedentary lifestyle, an unhealthy diet high in sugar and fat, family history, and ethnicity also increase the risk. Type 2 diabetes is more common in adults, and the rising rates of obesity mean it is becoming increasingly common worldwide.

Key Fact — Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes

Type 1: Pancreas does not produce insulin → treated with insulin injections → autoimmune, not lifestyle-related. Type 2: Body cells no longer respond to insulin → treated with diet and exercise → obesity is the main risk factor.

Interpreting Blood Glucose Data

Exam questions often show graphs comparing blood glucose levels in a healthy person, a person with Type 1 diabetes, and a person with Type 2 diabetes after a meal. In a healthy person, blood glucose rises after eating and then returns to normal within about two hours as insulin is released. In a person with Type 1 diabetes, the level rises steeply and stays high because no insulin is produced. In a person with Type 2 diabetes, the level rises and falls more slowly than normal because cells respond poorly to insulin.

When interpreting these graphs, describe what happens (the glucose level rises/falls), explain why (insulin is/is not produced or cells do/do not respond), and compare the rate and peak of the blood glucose changes between the individuals shown.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes, always state the cause, the treatment, and the risk factors for each. A common exam mistake is saying Type 2 diabetes means “the pancreas does not produce enough insulin” — the correct answer is that cells no longer respond to insulin. For negative feedback questions, describe the full loop: stimulus → receptor (pancreas) → hormone released → target organ response → condition returns to normal → hormone secretion reduces.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood to produce slower, longer-lasting responses than the nervous system. The pituitary gland is the master gland that controls other glands.
  • Blood glucose is controlled by insulin (lowers glucose, converts to glycogen) and glucagon (raises glucose, converts glycogen back to glucose) in a negative feedback cycle.
  • Type 1 diabetes = pancreas produces no insulin (treat with injections). Type 2 diabetes = cells do not respond to insulin (treat with diet/exercise). Obesity is the main risk factor for Type 2.

lessons.title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception
lessons.description: How FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone control the menstrual cycle, plus contraception and IVF.
lessons.content_html:
Hormones in Human Reproduction

The human endocrine system controls reproduction through a group of hormones produced by the pituitary gland and the ovaries. Understanding how these hormones interact is essential for this topic — the exam often asks you to describe the roles of individual hormones and explain how they control the menstrual cycle.

During puberty, the pituitary gland (a small gland at the base of the brain) begins releasing hormones that trigger the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In males, the testes produce testosterone, which stimulates sperm production and causes changes such as a deeper voice, facial hair, and increased muscle mass. In females, the ovaries begin producing oestrogen, which triggers egg maturation and changes such as breast development, widening of the hips, and the start of the menstrual cycle.

Key Fact

Four hormones control the menstrual cycle: FSH (follicle stimulating hormone), LH (luteinising hormone), oestrogen, and progesterone. FSH and LH are produced by the pituitary gland. Oestrogen and progesterone are produced by the ovaries.

The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle lasts approximately 28 days and is controlled by the interaction of the four key hormones. It prepares the body for pregnancy each month. If no fertilisation occurs, the cycle resets.

Days 1–4 — Menstruation: The uterus lining breaks down and is shed through the vagina as a period. Hormone levels are low at this stage.

Days 4–14 — Repair and build-up: FSH is released by the pituitary gland and causes an egg to mature inside a follicle in the ovary. The maturing follicle produces oestrogen, which causes the uterus lining to thicken with blood vessels, ready to receive a fertilised egg.

Day 14 — Ovulation: A surge in LH triggers ovulation — the release of the mature egg from the ovary into the fallopian tube. High oestrogen levels stimulate the pituitary gland to release this surge of LH.

Days 14–28 — Maintenance: After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and produces progesterone. Progesterone maintains the thick uterus lining. If no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone levels fall, and the lining is shed — the cycle starts again.

Hormone Interactions — Negative Feedback

The four hormones do not work in isolation — they interact through negative feedback. This means rising levels of one hormone can inhibit (reduce) the production of another, keeping the cycle in balance.

FSH stimulates oestrogen production. Rising oestrogen then inhibits further FSH release (so only one egg usually matures). At the same time, high oestrogen stimulates LH release, which triggers ovulation. After ovulation, progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH — preventing another egg from being released while the body waits to see if pregnancy occurs. When progesterone drops (because the corpus luteum breaks down), FSH is no longer inhibited and the cycle restarts.

Key Fact

Oestrogen inhibits FSH but stimulates LH. Progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH. This negative feedback loop ensures only one egg matures per cycle and prevents multiple ovulations.

Contraception

Contraception means preventing pregnancy. The specification requires you to know about hormonal and non-hormonal methods, and to be able to evaluate their effectiveness, side effects, and suitability.

Oral contraceptive pill: Contains hormones (oestrogen and/or progesterone). The combined pill contains both hormones — it prevents ovulation by maintaining high oestrogen and progesterone, which inhibits FSH and LH release. The progesterone-only pill thickens cervical mucus to prevent sperm reaching the egg. Effectiveness: over 99% if used correctly. Possible side effects include headaches, nausea, and blood clots (rare).

Contraceptive injection: A slow-release injection of progesterone given every 8–13 weeks. It inhibits ovulation and thickens cervical mucus. Very effective but cannot be reversed quickly once injected. May cause irregular periods.

Contraceptive implant: A small flexible rod inserted under the skin of the upper arm. It releases progesterone slowly for up to 3 years. Over 99% effective. May cause irregular bleeding in some users.

Contraceptive patch: A skin patch that releases oestrogen and progesterone through the skin. Changed weekly for three weeks, then a week off. Effectiveness: 99.8%. Side effects similar to the combined pill.

Condoms (male and female): Barrier methods that physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg. Condoms are 98% effective when used correctly and are the only method that also protects against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). No hormonal side effects.

Diaphragm or cap: A flexible dome placed over the cervix before sex. Used with spermicide. Around 92–96% effective. Must be fitted correctly and left in place for several hours after sex.

Intrauterine device (IUD): A small T-shaped device inserted into the uterus by a doctor. The copper IUD releases copper ions that are toxic to sperm and also prevents a fertilised egg from implanting. Over 99% effective and lasts 5–10 years. It is non-hormonal but can cause heavier periods.

Surgical methods: Sterilisation involves cutting or tying the fallopian tubes (female) or the vas deferens (male vasectomy). Permanent and highly effective. Difficult to reverse.

Abstinence and natural family planning: Avoiding sex during the fertile window (around ovulation). No side effects but requires careful monitoring of the cycle and is less reliable than other methods.

Key Fact

Hormonal contraception works by maintaining high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone, which inhibit FSH and LH through negative feedback — preventing ovulation. Barrier methods physically block sperm from reaching the egg. Only condoms protect against STIs.

The Use of Hormones to Treat Infertility (Higher Tier)

Infertility affects many couples. Hormones can be used to help women who have difficulty conceiving. Two main treatments involve reproductive hormones:

FSH and LH injections (fertility drugs): Women who do not ovulate naturally can be given FSH to stimulate egg maturation, followed by LH to trigger ovulation. This is called fertility treatment. A risk is that multiple eggs may be released, increasing the chance of multiple births (twins, triplets), which carry higher health risks for both mother and babies.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation): IVF is a more involved process. The woman is given FSH and LH to stimulate the ovaries to produce several eggs. These eggs are then collected surgically and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory dish. The fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and one or two are transferred into the woman’s uterus. Remaining embryos can be frozen for future use.

Benefits: IVF allows couples who cannot conceive naturally to have children. Success rates have improved over time. Embryos can be screened for genetic disorders before implantation. Unused embryos can be stored for later attempts.

Drawbacks: IVF is emotionally and physically demanding for the woman. Success rates are not guaranteed — typically around 30% per cycle for women under 35, lower for older women. The hormone treatment can cause side effects such as hot flushes, headaches, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. Multiple embryos may implant, leading to multiple births. There are ethical concerns about the fate of unused embryos — some people believe life begins at fertilisation and object to embryos being destroyed or frozen indefinitely. IVF is also expensive, with NHS funding varying by area.
lessons.exam_tip_html: AQA commonly asks you to compare contraceptive methods or evaluate IVF. For “compare and explain” questions, always state the similarity or difference clearly, then explain why using your knowledge of hormones. For extended response questions on IVF, structure your answer with benefits on one side and drawbacks on the other, and finish with a conclusion. Remember that IVF content is Higher Tier only — if you are sitting Higher, expect a question on it.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four hormones control the menstrual cycle: FSH and LH (from the pituitary gland) and oestrogen and progesterone (from the ovaries). They interact through negative feedback to regulate egg maturation, ovulation, and the uterus lining.
  • Hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy by inhibiting FSH and LH (so ovulation does not occur). Barrier methods physically block sperm. Only condoms protect against STIs.
  • IVF uses FSH and LH to stimulate egg production. Eggs are fertilised in a lab and embryos transferred to the uterus. Benefits include enabling conception; drawbacks include low success rates, side effects, and ethical concerns about unused embryos.

lessons.title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA
lessons.description: Sexual vs asexual reproduction, meiosis, gametes, DNA structure, and the human genome.
lessons.content_html:
Two Types of Reproduction

All living organisms reproduce to pass on their genes to the next generation. There are two fundamentally different ways this can happen: sexual reproduction and asexual reproduction. Understanding the differences between them is essential for AQA Biology Paper 2.

Sexual reproduction involves the fusion (joining together) of two special sex cells called gametes. In animals, the male gamete is the sperm cell and the female gamete is the egg cell (ovum). In plants, pollen contains the male gamete and the ovule contains the female gamete. When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, they form a single cell called a zygote, which then divides to form an embryo. Because each parent contributes different genetic information, the offspring show genetic variation — they are genetically unique.

Key Fact

Sexual reproduction produces offspring that are genetically different from each other and from both parents. This genetic variation is important because it helps populations adapt to changing environments through natural selection.

Asexual reproduction involves only one parent. There is no fusion of gametes. The offspring are produced by mitosis and are genetically identical to the parent — they are clones. Many organisms use asexual reproduction: bacteria divide by binary fission, plants can reproduce by runners or bulbs, and some animals such as starfish can regenerate from fragments.

Sexual reproduction: Two parents needed. Gametes fuse at fertilisation. Offspring are genetically varied. Involves meiosis. Slower process. Advantages — variation helps species survive environmental changes and resist disease.

Asexual reproduction: One parent only. No gamete fusion. Offspring are clones (genetically identical). Involves mitosis. Faster process. Advantages — only one parent needed, rapid population growth when conditions are favourable.

Some organisms, such as fungi, malarial parasites, and many plants, can switch between both types depending on conditions. When conditions are good, asexual reproduction is faster. When conditions change, sexual reproduction introduces variation that may help some offspring survive.

Meiosis — Making Gametes

Meiosis is the special type of cell division that produces gametes. It takes place in the reproductive organs — the ovaries and testes in animals, and the flower in plants. Meiosis is different from mitosis in several important ways.

Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs. These are called diploid cells. Before meiosis begins, the DNA replicates so that each chromosome is copied. The cell then divides twice: the first division separates the pairs of chromosomes, and the second division separates the copies. The result is four daughter cells, each with half the normal chromosome number — 23 chromosomes in humans. These cells are called haploid.

Key Fact

Meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells that are all genetically different. Mitosis produces two diploid daughter cells that are genetically identical. The AQA exam frequently asks you to compare these two types of cell division.

Meiosis introduces genetic variation in two ways. First, when chromosome pairs line up before the first division, they do so randomly — each gamete gets a different combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Second, sections of DNA can be swapped between paired chromosomes in a process called crossing over. These two mechanisms mean that every gamete produced by meiosis is genetically unique.

When a sperm cell (23 chromosomes) fuses with an egg cell (23 chromosomes) at fertilisation, the full diploid number is restored — the zygote has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). This is why gametes must be haploid: if they were diploid, the chromosome number would double with every generation.

DNA — The Molecule of Life

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made of two strands twisted into a double helix shape. Each strand is made of repeating units called nucleotides. A nucleotide consists of a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G).

The two strands of DNA are held together by complementary base pairing: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. This is why DNA can replicate accurately — each strand acts as a template for making a new complementary strand. The order of bases along a strand forms the genetic code that carries the instructions for building proteins.

DNA molecules are very long. In human cells, the DNA is tightly coiled and packed into structures called chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs — one chromosome in each pair comes from the mother and one from the father.

A gene is a short section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, which are assembled into a specific protein. Different genes code for different proteins, and it is these proteins that determine our characteristics — from eye colour to blood type to enzyme function.

Different versions of the same gene are called alleles. For example, the gene for eye colour has alleles for brown, blue, and green. Because chromosomes come in pairs, you inherit two alleles for every gene — one from each parent. Whether you display the characteristic depends on which alleles you have and whether they are dominant or recessive.

The Human Genome

The genome is the entire set of genetic material in an organism. The Human Genome Project was a major international research effort completed in 2003 that mapped the entire sequence of human DNA. Scientists identified approximately 20,000–25,000 genes across 3 billion base pairs of DNA.

Understanding the human genome has enormous benefits for science and medicine. It allows scientists to search for genes linked to specific diseases, develop personalised medicines that target an individual’s genetic makeup, trace human migration patterns across history, and identify how closely related different species are through evolutionary biology.

Key Fact

The Human Genome Project (completed 2003) identified all the genes in human DNA. Key benefits include: identifying genes linked to disease, developing targeted medicines, understanding evolutionary relationships, and advancing forensic science.

Medicine: Doctors can identify people who carry genes for inherited disorders (such as cystic fibrosis or Huntington’s disease) before symptoms appear. This enables genetic screening and counselling, and may lead to gene therapy treatments.

Pharmacogenomics: Medicines can be tailored to an individual’s genetic profile, making treatments more effective with fewer side effects. This is sometimes called personalised or precision medicine.

Evolution and ancestry: Comparing genomes of different species shows how closely related they are. More similar genomes indicate a more recent common ancestor. Scientists have also traced human migration out of Africa by studying patterns in modern genomes.

Forensics: DNA profiling uses specific sections of an individual’s genome to create a unique “genetic fingerprint,” used in criminal investigations and paternity testing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing sexual and asexual reproduction, always address both types — don’t just describe one. For 6-mark extended response questions on meiosis, structure your answer as a sequence: DNA replication → first division (pairs separate) → second division (copies separate) → four haploid cells. Always state the chromosome numbers (46 → 23 in humans). If asked about the importance of the genome, give specific examples of applications rather than vague statements like “it helps scientists.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sexual reproduction involves gamete fusion and produces genetically varied offspring; asexual reproduction uses mitosis and produces genetically identical clones.
  • Meiosis produces four haploid gametes (23 chromosomes each in humans) that are all genetically different — variation comes from random chromosome assortment and crossing over.
  • DNA is a double helix of nucleotides with complementary base pairs (A–T, C–G). Genes are sections of DNA on chromosomes, and different versions of genes are called alleles. The Human Genome Project mapped the entire human DNA sequence, enabling advances in medicine, forensics, and evolutionary biology.

lessons.title: Genetic Inheritance and Inherited Disorders
lessons.description: Punnett squares, dominant and recessive alleles, inherited disorders, and sex determination.
lessons.content_html:
Genetic Inheritance — The Basics

Every characteristic you inherit — from eye colour to blood type — is controlled by genes. Genes are short sections of DNA found on chromosomes in the nucleus of your cells. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total), with one chromosome in each pair inherited from each parent.

Most genes come in different versions called alleles. Because you have two copies of each chromosome (one from Mum, one from Dad), you carry two alleles for every gene. The combination of alleles you carry is your genotype, and the physical characteristic that results — what you can actually see — is your phenotype.

Key Fact

Genotype = the alleles you have (e.g. Bb). Phenotype = what you look like (e.g. brown eyes). The genotype determines the phenotype.

Dominant and Recessive Alleles

Some alleles are dominant — they are always expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present. Dominant alleles are written with a capital letter (e.g. B). Other alleles are recessive — they are only expressed when two copies are present (no dominant allele to “mask” them). Recessive alleles are written with a lowercase letter (e.g. b).

This gives three possible genotype combinations for any gene:

BB — homozygous dominant (two dominant alleles). Phenotype: dominant trait shown. Bb — heterozygous (one dominant, one recessive). Phenotype: dominant trait shown (the dominant allele masks the recessive). bb — homozygous recessive (two recessive alleles). Phenotype: recessive trait shown.

Key Fact

A heterozygous individual (Bb) is sometimes called a carrier of the recessive allele. They show the dominant phenotype but can pass the recessive allele to their children.

Punnett Squares

A Punnett square is a simple grid used to work out the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from a genetic cross. You place one parent’s alleles along the top and the other parent’s alleles down the side, then fill in the boxes to show every possible combination.

Imagine both parents are heterozygous (Bb) for a trait where B (brown eyes) is dominant over b (blue eyes).

Set up the Punnett square: Parent 1 alleles (B and b) go along the top. Parent 2 alleles (B and b) go down the side. Fill in the four boxes: BB, Bb, Bb, bb.

Results: 1 in 4 (25%) chance of BB (homozygous dominant — brown eyes). 2 in 4 (50%) chance of Bb (heterozygous — brown eyes). 1 in 4 (25%) chance of bb (homozygous recessive — blue eyes). Overall ratio of phenotypes: 3 brown : 1 blue.

Remember: these are probabilities, not guarantees. Having four children does not mean exactly three will have brown eyes and one blue — each child is an independent event.

Inherited Disorders

Some disorders are caused by faulty alleles that can be passed from parents to children. The specification requires you to know two inherited disorders: one caused by a dominant allele and one caused by a recessive allele.

Cystic Fibrosis (Recessive Disorder)

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). A person must inherit two copies of the faulty allele (ff) to have the disorder. People with the genotype Ff are carriers — they do not show symptoms but can pass the allele to their children.

Cystic fibrosis causes the body to produce thick, sticky mucus that clogs the lungs and digestive system. Symptoms include difficulty breathing, frequent lung infections, and problems digesting food. About 1 in 25 people in the UK carry the recessive allele.

If both parents are carriers (Ff), the Punnett square gives: FF (unaffected, not a carrier), Ff (carrier, unaffected), Ff (carrier, unaffected), ff (has cystic fibrosis).

Probability: 1 in 4 (25%) chance of having cystic fibrosis. 2 in 4 (50%) chance of being a carrier. 1 in 4 (25%) chance of being completely unaffected (FF). This means 3 in 4 (75%) of children will not show symptoms, but 2 out of those 3 will be carriers.

Polydactyly (Dominant Disorder)

Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (D). A person only needs one copy of the dominant allele (Dd or DD) to have the condition. This means an affected parent has at least a 50% chance of passing it to each child (if the affected parent is heterozygous, Dd).

Polydactyly causes a person to be born with extra fingers or toes. It is usually not life-threatening and the extra digits can often be surgically removed. Unlike cystic fibrosis, polydactyly cannot be “carried” without showing symptoms — if you have the dominant allele, you have the condition.

Key Fact

Cystic fibrosis = recessive (ff) — must inherit two faulty alleles; carriers (Ff) show no symptoms. Polydactyly = dominant (Dd or DD) — only one copy needed; no carriers exist because the allele is always expressed.

Sex Determination

In humans, biological sex is determined by the 23rd pair of chromosomes — the sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). All other chromosome pairs (1–22) are called autosomes.

Because a mother is XX, she can only pass on an X chromosome. A father is XY, so he can pass on either an X or a Y. This means the father’s sperm determines the sex of the child.

Mother’s alleles: X and X (along the top). Father’s alleles: X and Y (down the side). The four boxes give: XX, XX, XY, XY.

Result: 2 in 4 (50%) chance of being female (XX) and 2 in 4 (50%) chance of being male (XY). The probability is equal for each pregnancy — previous children’s sex has no effect on the next.

Key Fact

The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene, which triggers the development of male sex organs. Without the Y chromosome (i.e. XX), female development occurs by default.

Embryo Screening and Ethical Issues

During IVF or pregnancy, embryos and foetuses can be tested for inherited disorders such as cystic fibrosis. This is called genetic screening. It raises important ethical questions that the exam may ask you to discuss.

Arguments for screening: It prevents children being born with serious, life-limiting conditions. Parents can make informed choices about continuing a pregnancy. It reduces suffering for the child and family. It could eventually reduce the frequency of harmful alleles in the population.

Arguments against screening: Some people believe every embryo has a right to life regardless of genetic conditions. It could lead to a “designer baby” culture where embryos are selected for non-medical traits. The conditions tested for (like polydactyly) may not be life-threatening. Some religious groups believe only God should decide these matters. There is a risk of creating discrimination against people living with genetic conditions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In AQA Trilogy exams, you will often be given a Punnett square to complete or interpret. Always label your alleles clearly (capital for dominant, lowercase for recessive), show all four offspring genotypes, and state the probability as a ratio, fraction, or percentage. For “explain” questions about inherited disorders, make sure you state whether the allele is dominant or recessive, give the genotypes of affected individuals and carriers, and use a Punnett square if the question asks you to predict outcomes.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alleles are different versions of a gene. Dominant alleles (capital letter) are expressed with just one copy; recessive alleles (lowercase) need two copies to be expressed. Your genotype (alleles) determines your phenotype (what you look like).
  • Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (ff) — carriers (Ff) show no symptoms. Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (D) — only one copy is needed, so there are no carriers.
  • Sex is determined by the 23rd chromosome pair: XX = female, XY = male. The father’s sperm determines the sex of the child, with a 50:50 probability.

lessons.title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection
lessons.description: Variation, natural selection, fossils, extinction, and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Variation?

No two organisms are exactly alike — even identical twins have minor differences. Variation is the term for these differences between individuals of the same species. Variation matters because it is the raw material that natural selection acts on: without differences between organisms, evolution could not happen.

Variation is caused by two factors. Genetic variation results from differences in DNA inherited from parents. This includes features like eye colour, blood group, and the ability to roll your tongue. Environmental variation results from the conditions an organism lives in — for example, a plant grown in shade will be taller and thinner than the same species grown in full sunlight. Most characteristics are influenced by both genes and the environment. Height, for instance, is partly genetic but also affected by diet and health during childhood.

Key Fact

Variation can be genetic (caused by mutations, meiosis, and sexual reproduction), environmental (caused by conditions like diet, climate, or lifestyle), or both. Most human features — such as height, weight, and skin colour — are the result of a combination of genetic and environmental factors.

Mutations — The Source of New Variation

A mutation is a random change in the sequence of bases in DNA. Mutations happen continuously — every time a cell divides, its DNA is copied, and occasionally errors occur. Most mutations have no effect on the organism because they occur in non-coding regions of DNA or do not change the protein produced. Very rarely, a mutation leads to a new characteristic that gives the organism a survival advantage. These rare beneficial mutations are the driving force behind evolution.

Mutations can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial. A harmful mutation might produce a faulty protein that causes a genetic disorder. A beneficial mutation might help an organism survive better in its environment — for example, a mutation that makes a bacterium resistant to an antibiotic. The rate of mutation can be increased by exposure to certain environmental factors called mutagens, such as ionising radiation, ultraviolet light, and certain chemicals.

Natural Selection

Natural selection is the mechanism by which evolution occurs. It was first proposed by Charles Darwin after his voyage on HMS Beagle in the 1830s, where he observed variation between species on different islands — most famously the finches of the Galápagos, which had different beak shapes suited to different food sources.

Step 1 — Variation: Within any population, individuals show variation in their characteristics due to differences in their genes. A mutation may produce a new, advantageous trait.

Step 2 — Competition: Organisms compete for limited resources such as food, water, territory, and mates. Not all individuals will survive and reproduce.

Step 3 — Survival of the fittest: Individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive, find food, avoid predators, and resist disease. Darwin called this “survival of the fittest.”

Step 4 — Inheritance: The advantageous alleles are passed on to the next generation through reproduction. Over many generations, the beneficial allele becomes more common in the population — the species has evolved.

Key Fact

Natural selection can be remembered as: \(variation \rightarrow competition \rightarrow \text{survival of the fittest} \rightarrow inheritance\). Over many generations, advantageous alleles become more common and the species evolves. In exams, use the word “alleles” rather than “genes” for full marks.

Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is the process by which humans choose plants or animals with desirable characteristics and breed them together. Over many generations, the desired trait becomes more pronounced. Selective breeding has been used for thousands of years to produce food crops with higher yields, cattle that produce more milk, and dogs with particular temperaments or appearances.

Food plants: Wild wheat had small grains and was difficult to harvest. Over generations of selective breeding, farmers chose the plants with the largest grains and strongest stems. Modern wheat produces far more food per plant than its wild ancestor.

Dairy cattle: Cows that naturally produced more milk were bred together. Today, a modern dairy cow can produce over 20 litres of milk per day — far more than its wild relatives.

Dogs: All domestic dog breeds descend from wolves. Selective breeding over thousands of years has produced breeds ranging from Great Danes to Chihuahuas, each selected for different traits such as size, speed, herding instinct, or companionship.

The main disadvantage of selective breeding is that it reduces genetic variation within a population. Breeding closely related organisms together over many generations can lead to inbreeding, which increases the risk of inherited disorders and makes the population more vulnerable to new diseases — if all individuals are genetically similar, a single disease could wipe out the entire population.

Evidence for Evolution: Fossils

Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of organisms that lived thousands or millions of years ago. They are found in rocks, ice, peat bogs, and amber. Fossils provide crucial evidence that life on Earth has changed over time.

Fossils can form in three main ways. First, from the hard parts of organisms (bones, teeth, shells) that do not decay easily — these are gradually replaced by minerals over millions of years in a process called mineralisation. Second, as casts or impressions left in mud or sand that later turns to rock — footprints and leaf imprints are common examples. Third, by preservation in special conditions where decay cannot occur, such as in ice, peat bogs, or amber (tree resin), which prevent bacteria from breaking down the organism.

The fossil record shows how organisms have changed over time. Fossils of the simplest organisms are found in the oldest rocks, and fossils of more complex organisms appear in newer rocks. This supports the theory that simple life forms gradually evolved into more complex ones over billions of years. Scientists can also trace how specific features of a species have changed — for example, the evolution of the modern horse from a small, multi-toed ancestor to the large, single-hoofed animal we see today.

However, the fossil record is incomplete. Many early organisms were soft-bodied and decayed completely without leaving a trace. Some fossils have been destroyed by geological processes such as volcanic eruptions, tectonic movements, and erosion. Others simply have not been found yet. These gaps mean that scientists cannot always trace the full evolutionary history of every species.

Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria

Antibiotic-resistant bacteria provide some of the strongest and most observable evidence for natural selection happening in real time. Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop their growth. However, some bacteria have developed resistance to antibiotics — and this is a clear, real-world example of natural selection.

Step 1

Random mutation

Within a population of bacteria, a random mutation gives one bacterium resistance to a particular antibiotic.

Step 2

Antibiotic applied

The antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria, but the resistant bacterium survives because its mutation gives it a selective advantage.

Step 3

Reproduction

The resistant bacterium reproduces rapidly by binary fission (bacteria can divide every 20 minutes), passing the resistance allele to all its offspring.

Step 4

Resistant population

Over time, the entire population becomes resistant. The antibiotic is no longer effective, and a different treatment is needed.

Key Fact

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a well-known example of an antibiotic-resistant “superbug.” It is very difficult to treat and is a major problem in hospitals. To slow the development of resistance: doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when truly necessary; patients must always complete the full course; and antibiotics should not be used for viral infections (where they have no effect).

Extinction

Extinction occurs when there are no remaining individuals of a species alive anywhere on Earth. Over 99% of all species that have ever lived are now extinct — it is a natural part of the history of life. However, human activities have greatly increased the rate of extinction in recent centuries.

Species can become extinct due to several factors: a new predator that the species has no defence against; a new disease that spreads through the population; increased competition from a new species for the same resources; environmental changes such as climate change or habitat destruction that the species cannot adapt to quickly enough; or a catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption or asteroid impact. The mass extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago was caused by an asteroid impact that dramatically changed the global climate.

Species with low genetic variation are especially vulnerable to extinction. If all individuals in a population are genetically similar (for example, after extensive selective breeding or inbreeding), a single new disease or environmental change could kill the entire population because none of them carry the alleles needed to survive it. This is one reason why maintaining biodiversity and genetic diversity is so important.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark extended response questions on natural selection, always structure your answer as a clear sequence: variation exists within a population due to mutations → competition for resources → individuals with the best-adapted characteristics survive → they reproduce and pass on the advantageous allele → over many generations the population evolves. Use a specific example (such as antibiotic-resistant bacteria or peppered moths) and name the characteristic that gives the advantage. A common mistake is saying that organisms “choose” to change or “need” to adapt — natural selection is a random, unintentional process driven by variation and competition, not by the organism’s “choice.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Variation between individuals is caused by genetic factors (mutations, meiosis, sexual reproduction), environmental factors (diet, climate), or both — and mutations are the ultimate source of new genetic variation.
  • Natural selection follows a sequence: variation → competition → survival of the fittest → inheritance of advantageous alleles, leading to evolution over many generations.
  • Antibiotic-resistant bacteria (e.g. MRSA) are real-time evidence for natural selection; fossils show how organisms changed over geological time; and extinction removes species that cannot adapt to changing conditions.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology
lessons.description: Genetic engineering techniques, classification systems, and how organisms interact in ecosystems.
lessons.content_html:
Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering is a process where scientists modify the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from a different organism. This gives the modified organism a desirable characteristic it did not have before. The technique is used in agriculture, medicine, and industry.

The basic steps of genetic engineering are:

Step 1: The desired gene is identified and cut out of the DNA of one organism using restriction enzymes. These enzymes act like molecular scissors, cutting at precise recognition sequences in the DNA.

Step 2: The gene is inserted into a vector — usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus. The same restriction enzyme is used to cut the plasmid open, creating “sticky ends” that are complementary to the cut gene.

Step 3: Ligase is used to join the gene into the plasmid, sealing the sticky ends together. The vector then carries the gene into the target organism’s cells. The modified cells express the new gene and produce the desired protein or characteristic.

Key Fact

In genetic engineering, the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut both the gene of interest and the plasmid. This ensures the sticky ends are complementary and can be joined together by ligase.

GM crops are plants that have had their DNA altered to give them useful traits. Examples include crops engineered to be resistant to insect attack, resistant to herbicides, or able to produce higher yields. Golden rice has been engineered to produce beta-carotene to combat vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Benefits: GM crops can increase food production to help feed growing populations. They can reduce the need for chemical pesticides, lowering costs for farmers. Nutritional content can be improved — for example, golden rice provides vitamin A where diets lack it. Crops can also be engineered to survive harsh conditions such as drought or flooding.

Risks and concerns: GM crops could cross-pollinate with wild plants, creating herbicide-resistant “superweeds” that are difficult to control. There are concerns about long-term effects on human health, although no evidence of harm has been found so far. Reduced biodiversity may result if GM monocultures replace natural habitats. There are also ethical concerns about large corporations controlling seed supplies and farmers becoming dependent on them. The exam expects you to evaluate both sides of this debate.

Classification of Living Organisms

Scientists classify organisms into groups based on their similarities and differences. This makes it easier to study and identify millions of different species, understand evolutionary relationships, and monitor biodiversity. The traditional system was developed by Carl Linnaeus in the 18th century.

The Linnaean system organises organisms into a hierarchy of groups. From largest to smallest: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Each organism is given a two-part Latin name using its genus and species — this is called binomial nomenclature. For example, humans are Homo sapiens. The first name (genus) begins with a capital letter, and the species name is lowercase. The name is always written in italics or underlined when handwritten.

Key Fact

Carl Woese proposed the three-domain system by analysing the biochemistry of organisms, particularly differences in ribosomal RNA. The three domains — Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya — sit above the kingdom level and provide a more accurate picture of evolutionary relationships than the earlier five-kingdom model.

The three-domain system replaced the older five-kingdom model because advances in biochemistry and genome analysis showed the five-kingdom system was too simple. Archaea are primitive bacteria-like organisms often found in extreme environments — they are sometimes called extremophiles. Bacteria are true bacteria (eubacteria). Eukarya includes all organisms with cells containing a nucleus — animals, plants, fungi, and protists.

Evolutionary trees (phylogenetic trees) show the evolutionary relationships between organisms. They are built by comparing structural similarities, fossil evidence, and — more recently — DNA and protein analysis. Darwin first used these as a way to group organisms, although he did not know about genes.

On an evolutionary tree, species that are more closely related appear closer together. The further up the tree a branch point appears, the more recently those species diverged from a common ancestor. DNA evidence can reveal surprising relationships — for example, giant pandas are more closely related to bears than to red pandas, despite both eating bamboo.

Ecosystems and Communities

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment. Ecosystems can be as small as a rock pool or as large as the Amazon rainforest.

To understand ecosystems, you need to know these key terms precisely — you need to be able to tell them apart. A habitat is the place where an organism lives. A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area. A community is all the populations of different species living together in the same area.

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that affect where organisms can live. The main abiotic factors you need to know are: light intensity (affects photosynthesis and plant growth), temperature (affects enzyme activity and metabolic rate), moisture level (water availability for organisms), soil pH and mineral content (affects plant growth), wind speed and direction (affects transpiration and seed dispersal), and carbon dioxide levels (affects the rate of photosynthesis in plants).

Biotic factors are living factors that affect a community. Key biotic factors include: availability of food (limits population size), new predators arriving (reduces prey populations), new pathogens (cause disease and reduce populations), and competition between organisms for the same resources. A common exam error is mixing up abiotic and biotic — remember that abiotic means absence of life (non-living).

Competition and Interdependence

Organisms within a community depend on each other for survival — this is called interdependence. For example, bees depend on flowers for nectar, while flowers depend on bees for pollination. If one species is removed from a community, it can affect the whole food web.

Competition occurs when organisms compete for the same limited resources. Plants compete for light, water, space, and mineral ions from the soil. Animals compete for food, water, territory, and mates. Within a stable community, all the species and environmental factors are balanced so that population sizes remain roughly constant. Tropical rainforests and ancient oak woodlands are examples of stable communities.

Organisms have features called adaptations that help them survive in their environment. These develop over many generations through natural selection. There are three types:

Structural adaptations are physical features of an organism’s body. For example, the thick fur and small ears of an Arctic fox reduce heat loss in cold environments. Cacti have thick stems to store water and spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss by transpiration. Camels have large flat feet for walking on sand and thick eyelashes to protect against sandstorms.

Behavioural adaptations are actions organisms take to survive. For example, many birds migrate to warmer climates in winter to find food, and penguins huddle together to conserve heat.

Functional adaptations relate to internal body processes. For example, desert animals such as kangaroo rats produce very concentrated urine to conserve water. Some bacteria are extremophiles with enzymes that function at very high temperatures, allowing them to live in volcanic vents.

Key Fact

Extremophiles are organisms adapted to live in extreme environments such as high-temperature volcanic vents, very salty lakes, or high-pressure deep-sea habitats. Many extremophiles are classified as Archaea in the three-domain system.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on genetic engineering often ask you to describe the process step by step — make sure you name the enzymes (restriction enzymes to cut, ligase to join) and mention the vector (plasmid). For ecology questions, be precise with your terminology: don’t confuse “community” (all species in an area) with “population” (one species in an area). Extended response questions may ask you to evaluate GM crops — always give arguments for and against, with specific examples such as golden rice, before reaching a balanced conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genetic engineering uses restriction enzymes and ligase to cut, transfer, and insert genes from one organism into another via a vector such as a bacterial plasmid.
  • The three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) proposed by Carl Woese replaced the five-kingdom model, based on analysis of ribosomal RNA and biochemistry.
  • Ecosystems involve the interaction of communities with abiotic and biotic factors; organisms are interdependent and compete for limited resources; adaptations (structural, behavioural, functional) help organisms survive.

lessons.title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact
lessons.description: How ecosystems cycle materials, what threatens biodiversity, and how we can protect it.
lessons.content_html:
Levels of Organisation in an Ecosystem

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (the biotic components) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. To understand how ecosystems work, you need to know the hierarchy of organisation.

An individual organism is a single living thing. A population is all the organisms of one species in an area. A community is all the populations of different species in an area. An ecosystem includes both the community and the abiotic factors such as temperature, light, water, soil, and pH.

Key Fact

Remember the hierarchy: \(organism \rightarrow population \rightarrow community \rightarrow ecosystem\). Exam questions often ask you to define each level or explain the difference between a community and an ecosystem (a community is just the living organisms; an ecosystem also includes the abiotic environment).

Within an ecosystem, organisms compete for resources. Animals compete for food, territory, water, and mates. Plants compete for light, water, space, and mineral ions from the soil. Species that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce — this is natural selection at work within the ecosystem.

Abiotic factors (non-living) include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH, wind speed, carbon dioxide concentration, and oxygen levels in water. Changes in abiotic factors can affect the distribution and abundance of organisms — for example, plants grow faster in higher light intensities.

Biotic factors (living) include food availability, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and competition from other species. For example, the introduction of grey squirrels to the UK led to a decline in red squirrels because greys outcompete them for food and carry squirrel pox.

How Materials Are Cycled

Materials in an ecosystem are constantly recycled. Living organisms take in materials, use them, and return them to the environment when they die and decompose. Two key cycles you need to know are the carbon cycle and the water cycle.

The carbon cycle: Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis in plants and algae. Carbon is passed along food chains when animals eat plants and other animals. Carbon is returned to the atmosphere through respiration (by all living organisms), combustion of fossil fuels and wood, and decomposition of dead organisms by microorganisms. Some carbon becomes locked in fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) or sedimentary rocks (limestone) for millions of years.

The water cycle: Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and rivers, and transpires from plants. Water vapour rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds. Precipitation (rain, snow) falls back to the surface, where it flows into rivers or soaks into groundwater, eventually returning to the sea. This cycle is powered by energy from the sun.

Key Fact

Decomposition is essential to both cycles. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead plant and animal material, releasing carbon dioxide through respiration and returning mineral ions to the soil. Without decomposition, nutrients would be locked in dead organisms and unavailable for new growth.

What Is Biodiversity?

Biodiversity is the variety of all living species in an ecosystem or on Earth as a whole. High biodiversity means a wide range of different species are present. Ecosystems with high biodiversity are more stable and more resilient to environmental change because if one species is lost, others can fill its role in the food web.

Scientists measure biodiversity by studying the number of different species in an area (species richness) and the abundance of each species. To estimate population size in a habitat, scientists use sampling techniques such as quadrats placed randomly and transects to study distribution. Random sampling avoids bias and makes results more representative.

Quadrats: A 0.5m × 0.5m frame placed on the ground at random positions (using random number generators to pick coordinates). Count the number of organisms of each species inside the quadrat. Repeat in multiple positions and calculate a mean. To estimate total population: mean count per quadrat × total area ÷ area of one quadrat.

Transects: A measuring tape is laid in a straight line across a habitat (e.g. from a pond edge up a hillside). Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the line to record how species distribution changes with distance. This is useful for investigating the effect of an abiotic factor that changes across the habitat (e.g. light, moisture).

Human Threats to Biodiversity

The human population is growing rapidly, and our activities are reducing biodiversity worldwide. The spec identifies several key threats.

Waste management: Humans produce large quantities of waste. Unless properly handled, this pollutes water (sewage, fertiliser runoff causing eutrophication), air (smoke, acidic gases), and land (landfill, toxic chemicals). Pollution kills organisms directly and destroys habitats.

Land use: Building, quarrying, farming, and dumping waste all reduce the amount of land available for other organisms. As the human population grows, more land is converted for agriculture, housing, and industry, destroying natural habitats and reducing biodiversity.

Key Fact

Deforestation in tropical areas has severe consequences: loss of habitat for millions of species, release of stored carbon (increasing atmospheric CO₂), loss of trees that would absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis, and disruption of the water cycle (less transpiration means less rainfall). Large-scale deforestation in the Amazon and Southeast Asia is a major driver of both biodiversity loss and climate change.

Global warming: The burning of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, and farming livestock produces methane — both are greenhouse gases that trap heat in the Earth’s atmosphere. This leads to rising global temperatures, which cause sea level rise (from melting ice caps and thermal expansion), changes in the distribution of species, loss of polar habitats, more extreme weather events, and changes in migration patterns and breeding seasons.

Short-wave radiation from the sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The Earth re-emits this energy as long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapour) absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth. This keeps the planet warm enough to support life — the natural greenhouse effect. However, human activities have increased the concentration of greenhouse gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing average global temperatures to rise.

Maintaining Biodiversity

Scientists and governments recognise that biodiversity must be actively protected. The specification requires you to know programmes and strategies for maintaining biodiversity at local, national, and global levels.

Breeding programmes: Zoos and wildlife centres run captive breeding programmes for endangered species, then reintroduce them to the wild. Examples include the red kite in the UK and the Arabian oryx. Seed banks: Organisations like the Millennium Seed Bank store seeds from thousands of plant species to protect genetic diversity and allow future reintroduction if species become extinct in the wild.

Protected areas: National parks, nature reserves, and marine conservation zones protect habitats from development and allow ecosystems to recover. Hedgerow and habitat restoration: Farmers are encouraged (sometimes through government grants) to maintain hedgerows, field margins, and wildlife corridors that connect fragmented habitats.

Legislation: Laws such as the Wildlife and Countryside Act (1981) make it illegal to harm protected species or damage their habitats. Recycling and waste reduction: Reducing the amount of waste going to landfill limits habitat destruction and pollution. Sustainable development: Meeting the needs of the current population without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This includes sustainable forestry (replanting trees), sustainable fishing (quotas to prevent overfishing), and reducing carbon emissions through renewable energy.

Global agreements: International cooperation is essential because biodiversity loss and climate change are global problems. Agreements such as the Paris Agreement (2015) aim to limit global temperature rise. The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) restricts the trade of threatened animals and plants across borders.

Key Fact

The conflict between human needs and biodiversity is a common 6-mark question topic. You should be able to discuss how measures like breeding programmes, seed banks, protected areas, and legislation help maintain biodiversity — and acknowledge that these measures can conflict with economic development (e.g. farmers losing land to nature reserves, or industries restricted by environmental regulations).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For extended response questions on ecosystems and biodiversity, structure your answer clearly: state the problem (e.g. deforestation), explain the biological impact (loss of habitat, reduced biodiversity, increased CO₂), and then evaluate the solutions (breeding programmes, legislation, sustainable practices). Always use specific examples — naming real species, places, or laws scores higher than vague generalisations. For calculate questions on sampling, show your working and include units.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An ecosystem includes both the living community and the abiotic environment. Materials such as carbon and water are constantly recycled through decomposition, respiration, photosynthesis, and physical processes.
  • Human activities — waste, land use, deforestation, and burning fossil fuels — reduce biodiversity and contribute to global warming through increased greenhouse gas emissions.
  • Biodiversity can be maintained through breeding programmes, seed banks, protected areas, legislation, and international agreements — but these must balance conservation with human economic needs.
